title: Problem solving and mathematical writing
audience: a college student in a mathematics degree program (or a related major such as physics, computer science or economics), or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Learn to solve problems you have not seen before and to write mathematics clearly: strategies for unfamiliar problems (small cases, invariants, the extremal principle, symmetry, induction and the pigeonhole principle), inequalities, problems in number theory, combinatorics and algebra, writing proofs that others can follow, typesetting mathematics with LaTeX, and reading and presenting mathematics.
primary_reading: Book of Proof by Richard Hammack (free PDF)

weeks.1: How to attack an unfamiliar problem
weeks.6: The pigeonhole principle and counting arguments

blocks.deliverable: Solve three supplied problems and record every strategy you tried.
Use an invariant to prove that a supplied process can never reach a target state.
Write complete induction and pigeonhole proofs.
Week 7 midterm; prove two inequalities and solve a divisibility problem.
Rewrite a supplied messy proof so that a classmate can follow it.
Typeset a two-page solution set and present one solution aloud.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Problem portfolio: solve twelve problems from the supplied list, drawn from several areas, write each solution as a polished proof typeset in LaTeX with a paragraph on how you found it, and record a ten-minute presentation of your favorite solution for a peer.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
